meta.title: Buffett Value Stock Screener
meta.description: Scores US stocks using Warren Buffett and Benjamin Graham's quantitative criteria

common.disclaimer: Not investment advice. All scores and intrinsic value estimates are reference calculations only — do not use them as the sole basis for investment decisions.

glossary.universe: How many stocks this site has scored and analysed. The universe is the S&P 500 — the 500 largest, most established US companies.
glossary.buyCandidate: A stock that scores well AND looks cheaper than our estimate of what it's worth. It isn't a recommendation to buy — it just means it's worth a closer look.
glossary.avgScore: The average total score (out of 100) across every stock analysed. A stock scoring above this number is doing better than typical.
glossary.undervalued: How many of the stocks trade below what they're estimated to be worth — that is, how many have a positive margin of safety.
glossary.stock: The company's name and its ticker — the short code it trades under (for example, Apple is AAPL).
glossary.sector: The industry the company operates in. Normal levels of profit and debt differ by industry, so it's only fair to compare companies within the same sector.
glossary.price: The price of one share. This is a delayed quote (typically 15+ minutes), not a live one.
glossary.marketCap: What the whole company is worth: share price × number of shares. B means billion dollars, T means trillion.
glossary.total: Quality, growth, financial health, consistency, and valuation are each scored out of 100, then blended by how much each matters. The higher it is, the more it looks like a good business available at a fair price.
glossary.marginOfSafety: In one line: how big a discount you're getting. If a share works out to be worth $100 and it's trading at $70, you're paying $30 (30%) less than it's worth — that 30% is the margin of safety. It's the cushion that limits the damage if the $100 estimate turns out to be off, which is why it's called a margin of *safety*. Bigger is cheaper; a negative number means the stock costs more than it's worth.
glossary.intrinsicValue: In one line: what one share is actually worth, estimated from the cash the business is likely to generate. It's separate from the price the market is charging today — the gap between the two is the margin of safety. Remember it's an estimate that moves with its assumptions, not a fact.
glossary.currentPrice: What one share is trading for right now.
glossary.priceAtFavorite: The share price on the day you tapped the heart to add this stock to your favorites.
glossary.change: Today's price compared with the price on the day you favorited it. Green + means it's up since then; red − means it's down.
glossary.favoritedAt: The date you added this stock to your favorites.
glossary.priceChart: How the share price has moved over time. Each bar is one day, and the toolbar on the left lets you draw your own trend lines.

portfolio.title: My Portfolio
portfolio.tip: A watchlist says "I'm following this"; a portfolio says "this much of my money is in it". Those are different questions — a 12% loss on a 2% position and the same loss on a 40% position are not the same event, and nothing here could tell them apart before. Enter shares and average cost and the market value, return, weight and sector exposure become real numbers.
portfolio.empty: No positions yet. Use "Add position" above to start.
portfolio.upsertNote: Saving a ticker you already hold replaces the existing row. Lot-level tracking is a separate feature for tax reporting and isn't handled here.
portfolio.axisProfileTip: Each company's axis scores weighted by its share of the portfolio's market value — not a plain average, which would give a $200 leftover position the same say as one that is 90% of the account.
portfolio.unscored: {tickers} aren't in the current snapshot, so they can't be scored. They count toward market value but are excluded from the weighted scores.
portfolio.note: Current price is the live quote where it could be fetched, and the last batch price where it couldn't. Taxes, commissions and dividends are not reflected.

fields.notePlaceholder: e.g. bought in tranches through the 2024 selloff

errors.sharesPositive: Shares must be greater than zero.

summary.weightedScoreTip: Each holding's total score weighted by its share of market value. Holdings that can't be scored are left out entirely and the rest renormalised, rather than counted as zero.

breakers.title: Thesis Breakers
breakers.tip: This is not a price alert. A share falling 30% is something your broker already tells you, and it says nothing about whether the business changed. This watches the other thing: conditions you decided in advance would undo your reasoning, checked against the company's current numbers every time you open this page. The rules take the same form as the screen builder on the dashboard.
breakers.empty: No rules yet. Load the defaults or add your own below. Rules apply to everything you hold and everything you've favorited.
breakers.allClear: Nothing has broken across the {count} companies being watched.
breakers.unmeasurable: {count} rules couldn't be checked — this company's filing doesn't carry those figures.
breakers.note: Nothing breaking doesn't mean nothing is wrong. These are the rules you set, checked against figures as of the last batch run.

alertSettings.title: Alert thresholds
alertSettings.tip: What counts as a change depends on how closely you're watching — someone holding six companies wants a finer setting than someone scanning sixty. Changing these recomputes the watchlist alerts above.
alertSettings.current: Current — total {total} pts · single axis {axis} pts · price down {price}% · compared against {days} days ago
alertSettings.note: Defaults are 5 points total, 12 per axis, a 25% price fall, and 30 days. Thirty days is roughly the gap between quarterly filings landing; anything tighter mostly reports the share price nudging the valuation axis around.

totalThreshold.label: Total score
totalThreshold.tip: Report a move of at least this many points in the total score. Lower means more alerts.

axisThreshold.label: Single axis
axisThreshold.tip: Report a move of at least this many points in any one of the five axes. Catches a business whose quality is eroding while the total holds steady.

priceDropThreshold.label: Price drop
priceDropThreshold.tip: Report a fall of at least this much from the price when you favorited it. Falls only — a rally is already reported from the other direction by the margin-of-safety alerts.

lookbackDays.label: Compare against
lookbackDays.tip: How far back to compare. Uses the most recent record older than this.

dashboard.title: Buffett Value Stock Screener
dashboard.subtitle: Scores every S&P 500 stock using Warren Buffett and Benjamin Graham's quantitative criteria (ROE, ROIC, debt ratio, earnings consistency, margin of safety, and more).
dashboard.fixtureBanner: ⚠️ You're viewing sample (fictional) data. To switch to real data, run npm run refresh — no setup or API key needed. See the README for details.
dashboard.emptyState: No score data yet. Run npm run refresh to generate it.

table.partialCoverage: Graded on the {percent}% of this axis the filing supplied. The dotted underline marks this.

strategy.title: Screen by your own conditions
strategy.tip: Where the weight sliders change how the scores are combined, this sets which underlying numbers a company has to clear. Conditions combine with AND — only companies meeting every one of them remain. Each figure is the same one printed in the criteria tables on a company's own page, so you can always check why something was filtered out.
strategy.empty: No conditions yet. Pick one of the examples above, or add your own below.
strategy.missingDataTip: Companies whose filings don't carry one of the figures you asked about, so the condition can't be applied at all. They didn't fail the screen — the question couldn't be answered — and they're excluded from the results.

weights.title: Adjust weights
weights.tip: The defaults are Quality 30% · Valuation 25% · Financial Health 20% · Growth 15% · Consistency 10%. Move the sliders to set the five axes' relative importance yourself, and the total score and ranking recompute against that. Prefer stability over growth? Raise Financial Health. Everything runs in this browser only — nothing is saved to the server — and persists on this device the next time you open the page.
weights.customTip: The total shown here is recomputed using the weights you set above, not the defaults (Quality 30% · Valuation 25% · Financial Health 20% · Growth 15% · Consistency 10%).

widgets.avgScoreTip: The average total score across every screened stock, independent of the current filters.
widgets.buyCandidateTip: The Buy Candidate with the largest margin of safety.
widgets.buyCandidateEmpty: No stock currently meets the Buy Candidate bar.
widgets.topMarginOfSafetyTip: The 5 stocks with the largest margin of safety.

stock.chartUnavailableHint: An ad blocker, a network issue, or HTTPS inspection by locally installed security software can all cause this. If reloading doesn't help, try another device.

chartHelp.summary: Chart still not showing? See how to fix it
chartHelp.step1: Start with a hard reload (Ctrl + F5). If that doesn't help, try a different browser (Chrome, Edge, Safari).
chartHelp.step2: Turn off ad blockers (AdBlock, uBlock Origin, AdGuard) for this site, or allowlist it. The chart is loaded from TradingView, which some block lists cover.
chartHelp.step3: Open https://s3.tradingview.com/tv.js directly in a new tab. If you see "Your connection is not private" or NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID, the HTTPS (SSL) inspection feature of security software installed on your computer is the cause.
chartHelp.step4: If step 3 applies, open that security program's settings and either disable HTTPS/SSL inspection or add tradingview.com as an exception.
chartHelp.step5: On a corporate or school network, a firewall may be blocking it. If the chart loads fine over mobile data, it's a network issue.
chartHelp.step6: Even if none of the above works, the Open in TradingView button below shows the same chart in a new window. Scores and financial data are unaffected.

stock.chartDrawingsNote: To keep your trend lines permanently, sign in to TradingView and open the chart via "Open in TradingView". The chart embedded here is TradingView's free widget, so drawings aren't stored against your account on this site.

dcf.title: Intrinsic Value & Margin of Safety
dcf.ownerEarningsNote: Based on owner earnings of {value} per share, a 5-year growth rate of {growth}, a {discount} discount rate, and a {terminal} terminal growth rate.
dcf.negativeOwnerEarnings: Owner earnings (operating cash flow minus capital expenditure) have been negative over the last three years, so the discounted cash flow model does not apply. This is routine for capital-intensive utilities and infrastructure and does not by itself mean the business is troubled — but it cannot be valued this way, so the margin-of-safety criterion scores at the floor.

fairValue.title: Fair Value (Multiple Methods)
fairValue.tip: A single valuation method on screen looks more certain than it is — move the DCF growth assumption by two points and the answer moves 30%. So four methods are shown separately alongside their weighted blend. How far apart they land (the range bar below) is itself the reading: estimates clustered together mean something; estimates 3x apart mean no single number here is worth trusting.
fairValue.weightedTip: A weighted blend of the four methods (DCF 40% · own P/E 25% · Graham 20% · sector P/E 15%). When a method's inputs are missing, its weight is redistributed proportionally across the rest.
fairValue.wideSpread: These methods disagree by {ratio}×. At that distance they are effectively measuring different things, so the blended figure should not be read as a target price. Look at each method's assumptions below and judge which one fits this company.
fairValue.note: All four methods are computed from the scoring data already on this page — no new external data, and the Buffett Score itself is unaffected by any of it. P/FCF and EV/EBITDA are excluded because the snapshot doesn't store those figures; including them would mean changing the scoring logic and recomputing all 503 tickers.
fairValue.methodUnavailable: The filing doesn't carry what this method needs, so it wasn't computed. Its weight went to the other methods.

assumptions.historicalPe: Own 5-year average P/E of {pe}× earnings per share of {eps}
assumptions.sectorPe: Sector average P/E of {pe}× earnings per share of {eps}
assumptions.graham: √(22.5 × EPS × book value per share). Graham's rule of thumb, from 1949.

reverseDcf.label: Reverse DCF —
reverseDcf.body: For today's price to be right, owner earnings would have to grow {implied} a year for the next five years. The forward DCF assumed {assumed}. Where the implied rate exceeds the assumption, the market is expecting this company to grow faster than it has.

thesis.title: Investment Thesis (Bull / Bear)
thesis.tip: No language model wrote any of this. It is derived by rule from the scoring criteria at the bottom of this page: a criterion earning 75% or more of its points becomes a strength, 35% or less a weakness. They are ordered by how much each one actually decided of the 100-point total — so what matters most comes first, rather than what reads most dramatically.
thesis.watchNote: These sit between the pass and fail lines, close enough that the next filing could move them either way.
thesis.bullEmpty: No criterion earned 75% or more of its points.
thesis.bearEmpty: No criterion fell to 35% or less of its points.
thesis.inconclusive: Neither case is clear. Most criteria land in the middle band, so this company does not resolve to one side.
thesis.method: Criteria we could not measure appear on neither side. A number the filing does not carry is not the company's failing, so it is not counted against it. Every figure here can be checked against the criteria tables below.

risk.negativeEquity: Book equity is negative. Both heavy buyback franchises and genuinely distressed companies land here, and the score cannot tell them apart. Worth checking directly.
risk.lossYears: {years} of the {total} fiscal years on record were losses.
risk.highLeverage: Net debt is {value}× EBITDA. Above roughly 3× this becomes a burden in a downturn.
risk.negativeOwnerEarnings: Owner earnings per share are {value} — negative. Capital spending exceeds the cash coming in (routine for regulated utilities), which means the DCF intrinsic value model does not apply here at all.
risk.dilution: Share count grew {value}. Existing holders own a smaller slice regardless of how the business performed.
risk.aboveIntrinsicValue: The current price is {value} above estimated intrinsic value. There is no margin of safety.
risk.lowCoverage: Only {percent}% of the {axis} axis could be read from the filing, so that axis score rests on thin evidence.

news.title: Recent News (last 30 days)
news.empty: No related news in the last 30 days.

history.title: Score History
history.tip: Each quarter-end is re-scored from the filings that were actually public on that date and that day's share price. If quality held steady while the valuation score rose, the business didn't improve — the stock got cheaper.
history.backfillNote: Past scores are recalculated with today's formula from the data available at the time.

quality.name: Quality
quality.tip: How good the business itself is: how much it keeps from every sale (margins), how much it earns on the capital it uses (ROE/ROIC), and whether it returns cash to shareholders.

growth.name: Growth
growth.tip: Whether the business is getting bigger — how fast revenue, earnings, and cash have grown over the last five years. Without growth, time doesn't work in your favour no matter how cheaply you buy.

health.name: Financial Health
health.tip: Whether debt could sink it. This is the balance sheet's ability to survive a bad year — the reason Buffett insists on companies that owe little.

consistency.name: Consistency
consistency.tip: Whether results are steady and predictable. Buffett won't buy a company whose future earnings he can't reasonably estimate, however good it looks today.

valuation.name: Valuation
valuation.tip: Whether today's price is cheap relative to what the business is worth. Even a great company won't return much if you overpay for it.

roe.label: Return on Equity (ROE), 5-yr avg
roe.explanation: Buffett's most-watched metric — how efficiently a company turns shareholder equity into profit.

roic.label: Return on Invested Capital (ROIC), 5-yr avg
roic.explanation: Return on all capital including debt — stays high in companies with a durable economic moat.

grossMargin.label: Gross Margin — level & stability
grossMargin.explanation: Companies with pricing power keep gross margins high and don't see them swing much year to year.

operatingMargin.label: Operating Margin, 5-yr avg
operatingMargin.explanation: What's left from the core business on every dollar of sales — the higher it is, the more the company sets its own prices.

fcfMargin.label: Free Cash Flow Margin
fcfMargin.explanation: The share of revenue that ends up as actual cash — far harder to dress up than accounting profit.

shareCount.label: Share Count Trend (buybacks)
shareCount.explanation: A signal of shareholder-friendly capital allocation.

revenueCagr.label: Revenue Growth (5-yr CAGR)
revenueCagr.explanation: Whether the company is actually selling more. Flat revenue with rising profit often means it's living on cost cuts.

epsCagr.label: EPS Growth (5-yr CAGR)
epsCagr.explanation: How fast the earnings attributable to each share are growing.

fcfCagr.label: Free Cash Flow Growth (5-yr CAGR)
fcfCagr.explanation: Whether real cash generation is expanding — the number intrinsic value is built on.

debtToEquity.label: Debt / Equity
debtToEquity.explanation: How much it owes against what the owners put in. Lower means an easier time surviving a downturn.

interestCoverage.label: Interest Coverage
interestCoverage.explanation: How many times over operating profit covers the interest bill. Below 1x the company isn't even earning its interest.

currentRatio.label: Current Ratio
currentRatio.explanation: Short-term liquidity — can the company withstand a sudden cash crunch?

netDebtToEbitda.label: Net Debt / EBITDA
netDebtToEbitda.explanation: How many years of cash earnings it would take to clear the debt left after subtracting cash on hand.

cashToDebt.label: Cash / Debt
cashToDebt.explanation: How much of the debt could be repaid from cash on hand today — ∞ means no debt at all.

epsPositiveYears.label: Profitable Years
epsPositiveYears.explanation: How many of the recent years were free of losses — Buffett's "predictable earnings" test.

fcfPositiveYears.label: Cash-Positive Years
fcfPositiveYears.explanation: Whether cash generation held up year after year, rather than in one or two good years.

revenueConsistency.label: Revenue Growth Consistency
revenueConsistency.explanation: How many years revenue rose over the prior one — steady beats erratic.

peRelative.label: P/E vs. own history & sector
peRelative.explanation: How cheap the stock is relative to earnings, compared against its own history and its sector.

peg.label: PEG Ratio
peg.explanation: Valuation relative to growth — below 1 suggests undervalued relative to growth.

grahamNumber.label: Price vs. Graham Number
grahamNumber.explanation: √(22.5 × EPS × Book Value/Share) — Graham's classic upper bound for a fairly priced stock.

marginOfSafety.label: Margin of Safety (vs. DCF intrinsic value)
marginOfSafety.explanation: Discount to intrinsic value estimated via a simple owner-earnings DCF — the core Graham/Buffett principle.

dataSource.tip: Financial figures come from the filings the company submits to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. "Trailing 12 months" means the year ending at the most recent quarter; "fiscal year" means the last annual report, with no quarter since folded in. Prices refresh once a day and are not live.
dataSource.coverageTip: The share of this axis that the filing actually supplied. Companies report different line items — a bank has no gross margin or current ratio — so some criteria cannot be calculated. Below 100%, the axis was graded on what was found; below half, it is graded against half the points regardless, so a thin sample cannot inflate the score.
dataSource.unavailableReason: This company's filings do not carry the figure this criterion needs. Scoring it zero would claim we looked and the answer was bad, so it is left out of the axis entirely.

peers.title: Sector comparison
peers.tip: A score of 62 means little on its own — a bank and a software company are graded on the same five axes but land in very different ranges. This shows where the company sits among its GICS sector. The vertical line on each bar is the sector median: a bar past the line is above the middle of its field.
peers.lowCoverage: Some axes for this company were graded on the {percent}% its filings supplied.
peers.caveat: The table lists the companies closest in market capitalisation — a $2T company and an $8B one in the same sector are not really in the same business. "Period" is the date each company's figures run to; fiscal calendars differ, so these can be up to a year apart. Retailers in particular show different leverage at different quarter ends because of inventory and payables cycles. An asterisk marks a company with criteria we could not measure.

backtest.title: Backtest
backtest.subtitle: If you had re-selected this site's three built-in strategies (Buy Candidate, Top 20, Universe) at the start of every quarter, here's what you'd actually have earned — lined up against the real S&P 500 index (SPY).
backtest.survivorshipBanner: Survivorship bias warning — this backtest applies today's S&P 500 constituent list to every past date. A company that was in the index in 2023 but has since been dropped for poor performance never appears in any past calculation. That means the returns below are systematically higher than reality — the underperformance of every company that got kicked out of the index is entirely missing. Not investment advice.
backtest.scopeNote: Covers 13 realized quarter-to-quarter transitions, from 2023-03-31 to 2026-06-30, recomputed at each quarter-end. Daily forward score history is still too thin to backtest at finer granularity — this will only get richer, and cover longer stretches, as more of it accumulates.
backtest.chartHint: Move across the chart to see that quarter's values.
backtest.emptyState: No backtest data yet. Run npm run backtest (it needs quarterly score history from npm run backfill first).

tip.totalReturn: If you'd put money into this strategy on March 31, 2023, this is how much it would have grown by June 30, 2026. Price return only — dividends aren't included.
tip.cagr: Turns a multi-year return into 'what steady rate, compounded every year, would get the same result.' For example, +33% over 3 years works out to roughly +10% a year, compounded. There's only about 3 years of data here, so one or two strong or weak quarters can swing this a lot — don't read it as a long, proven track record.
tip.maxDrawdown: If you'd held this strategy the whole time, this is the worst peak-to-trough drop you'd have had to sit through — for example -20% means your holdings were once down 20% from their high point before recovering. But this figure is measured only at quarter-ends, so it comes out far smaller than the fall you'd actually have lived through. Over this same window SPY reads -8.0% at quarter-ends but -19.0% on daily closes (trough April 8, 2025): a drop that opened and largely recovered inside one quarter is invisible to quarter-end sampling. The -19% is the one you'd have felt.
tip.quarters: How many quarters this strategy finished up versus down. Every quarter, the strategy is fully re-selected from scratch using that quarter's data (rebalancing) — a stock that drops out of Buy Candidate is no longer held the next quarter.
tip.holdings: The range of how many tickers this strategy actually held from quarter to quarter. Fewer holdings (say, under 20) means one or two big movers can swing the whole strategy's result more — since every position gets an equal dollar amount, holding count is a direct measure of how much any single stock matters.
tip.universe: Every scored company held in equal dollar amounts, regardless of size. This is NOT the real S&P 500 — the real index is market-cap-weighted (bigger companies count for more), so in a stretch like the last few years where a handful of mega-caps drove most of the index's gains, this equal-weight result can lag the real index.
tip.spy: The real, survivorship-bias-free market return, computed from the actual traded price of the S&P 500 tracking ETF (ticker: SPY). This is the only genuine benchmark on this page — the other three are internal strategies, not real indexes.
tip.chart: Each strategy starts at 100 and compounds its quarterly return forward. A higher line means more growth by that point. Click a legend chip to toggle a strategy on or off.
tip.sharpe: Return divided by how bumpy the ride was to get it. Same return, less volatility along the way, higher number. With only ~3 years of quarterly data, treat this as a rough read, not a settled figure.

yearlyReturns.title: Yearly Returns (Top 20)
yearlyReturns.note: Bucketed from quarterly data starting 2023, so there are only a few bars.

alerts.title: What changed
alerts.empty: Nothing notable lately. Sharp score moves and Buy Candidate changes show up here.
alerts.backfilled: comparison point is a reconstructed score
alerts.tip: There is no email or push here. Instead, each watched company is compared against its own past, and the changes worth a second look are collected here. Price moves are already in every broker app; what matters here are the changes that quietly undo the reason you were interested — the balance sheet deteriorating, the margin of safety closing, a company dropping out of Buy Candidate.
alerts.caveat: Compared against the most recent score at least 30 days old; each item names the date it was compared with. Points computed under different formula versions are not compared — that difference is us changing, not the company.

insiderTrading.title: Insider Trading (Form 4)
insiderTrading.tip: A company's officers, directors, and anyone owning 10%+ of its stock are legally required to report to the SEC within two business days whenever they buy or sell shares of their own company (Form 4). The table below shows their most recent reported trades.
insiderTrading.caveat: A purchase is often read as a positive signal, since it means an insider is spending their own money — but a sale is much weaker evidence of anything. Insiders sell for all kinds of reasons unrelated to their view of the company: diversification, taxes, a scheduled 10b5-1 plan, buying a house. Don't read a sale as bearish the way a purchase is often read as bullish. This table also covers only plain share transactions bought or sold on the market — not option grants or RSU vesting.

dca.title: Dollar-Cost Averaging Simulator
dca.tip: Simulates buying a fixed dollar amount of this stock on a repeating schedule and shows what it would be worth today. Reflects price moves only — no trading fees, taxes, or dividends.

form.note: Picking a day that doesn't exist in a given month (like the 31st) buys on that month's last day instead. If the market's closed, the purchase uses the next trading day's close.

stats.returnTip: (current value − total invested) / total invested. Excludes dividends, fees, and taxes.

dca.emptyState: No purchases under these settings — check the start date.
